AFG.story:
During the war in Afghanistan, commanders in the Afghan security forces and the Afghan Local Police sexually abused boys, a practice known as bacha bazi. In 2011 two US soldiers, Capt. Dan Quinn and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland, beat a local police commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy. Quinn was relieved of his command and Martland was at first discharged. In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told not to intervene when their Afghan allies abused boys, in some cases even on US bases.

Nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR), the US official who audits spending in Afghanistan, to investigate. Its report, made public in January 2018, found that by August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them sexual assaults on children. A US law, the Leahy Law, requires aid to be cut to military units that commit such violations, but the Pentagon used an exception in the law to keep supporting them. In December 2015 it approved continued funding for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.

After the Taliban took power, the UN verified sexual violence against 13 children in 2022, 12 in 2023 and 6 in 2024, and attributed most of these cases to the Taliban. In March 2024 boys aged 10 to 17 at Taliban-run madrasahs, religious schools, told the broadcaster Radio Azadi that teachers had pressured them into sexual acts. One 16-year-old reported a teacher to the school's qari, a senior religious teacher, who only told the teacher to stop, and the abuse continued. The Taliban run 6,836 madrasahs for boys and have sought 100,000 new teachers for them.

Under the former government and under the Taliban, boys have been abused by men with official power, and the United States kept funding units accused of it. The UN's small yearly counts are the only figures, and no representative survey has measured online sexual exploitation of children in South Asia.

BEN.story:
Among the Fon people of Benin, and the Ewe in neighbouring Ghana and Togo, some traditional shrines practise trokosi. A family gives a girl, usually a young virgin, to a shrine to atone for a wrong that a relative is said to have committed. The girl serves the shrine's priest without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as part of her duty, which defenders of the practice deny. Ghana made ritual servitude a crime in 1998, with a minimum sentence of three years, but the practice continued there and the source records no prosecutions. The records for this map do not describe any law or prosecution in Benin.

There is also no survey that measures the sexual exploitation of children in Benin. Childlight, a research centre that combines national surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa had no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children.

How many girls are held in shrines in Benin, and how many children are exploited in other ways, is not known.

BHR.story:
The records for this map hold no case, inquiry or count of child sexual abuse or trafficking in Bahrain. Childlight, a research centre that combines national surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that there was no representative survey data on the online sexual exploitation of children for the Middle East and North Africa, the region that includes Bahrain. Without such surveys, the only figures for a country are the cases that reach its police or that technology companies report.

The extent of child sexual exploitation in Bahrain is therefore not known.
---

CAF.story:
In December 2013 France sent soldiers to the Central African Republic in Operation Sangaris, under French and not UN command. Six boys aged 9 to 13 later told UN staff that French soldiers had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the camp for displaced people at M'Poko airport in Bangui, in exchange for food rations. The UN did not pass its internal report to the French authorities, and Anders Kompass, the UN official who did, was suspended and resigned in 2016. The Paris prosecutor's investigation grew to cover accusations by 15 children, but in January 2018 French judges closed the case for lack of sufficient evidence, and no soldier was charged.

The UN's own mission, MINUSCA, faced similar accusations. Under UN rules, only the country that sends a peacekeeper can prosecute them, and the UN can only send soldiers home. Two allegations about Gabonese and Burundian troops in Dékoa led to interviews with about 136 alleged victims, 48% of all victims the UN recorded worldwide in 2016. Press reports said 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges. In 2015 girls in Bambari told Human Rights Watch they had been raped by peacekeepers guarding the airport, and in January 2016 the UN withdrew a battalion from the Democratic Republic of the Congo whose soldiers had been accused of rape. In September 2021 it sent home all of Gabon's units, about 450 soldiers, after more allegations.

In 2024 the UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in the country: 58 by the CPC coalition of armed groups and 35 by government and pro-government forces. It also verified the abduction of 141 children, most of them for recruitment or sexual violence.

None of the foreign soldiers accused of abusing children in the Central African Republic is recorded here as convicted. The country's own forces are now among those the UN finds abusing girls, and no survey has measured the abuse of children across West and Central Africa.

CHN.story:
China opened intercountry adoption, the adoption of its children by parents in other countries, in 1992. About 160,000 children were sent abroad, most of them to the United States, which issued visas to 87,704 children adopted from China between 1994 and 2014. Between 2002 and 2005 six state orphanages in Hunan province bought babies from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with families in China and abroad. In 2005, 23 officials were fired and three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years in prison. The New Yorker reported that the programme came to depend more and more on abuse, abduction and trafficking, and on 5 September 2024 China ended it.

From 2017, as hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the authorities built boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitories. Records showed that more than 400 children in one township had lost both parents to internment or prison. The New York Times reported that about 497,000 pupils were enrolled in such schools in 2019. A Xinjiang official denied that the state was caring for large numbers of children without parents.

Girls and women are also brought into China from neighbouring countries and sold as brides. Human Rights Watch reported in 2019 that women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States in Myanmar, many displaced by war, were sold to Chinese families for US$3,000 to $13,000, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. Pakistan's Federal Investigation Agency listed 629 girls and women sold to Chinese men from 2018 to mid-2019. Officials told the AP news agency that the investigation largely stopped because of pressure from officials worried about relations with Beijing, and in October 2019 a court in Faisalabad acquitted 31 Chinese nationals.

In 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports of online abuse from technology companies, received 9,406 reports for China, compared with 1,933,900 for India, because most American platforms are blocked there. The extent of online abuse of children in China is therefore not known, and the trade in brides from neighbouring countries continues.

CIV.story:
Farms in Côte d'Ivoire and neighbouring Ghana supply cocoa to international chocolate companies. In the 2001 Harkin-Engel Protocol and again in 2010, the industry committed to cut the worst forms of child labour in cocoa by 70 percent by 2020. A study by NORC at the University of Chicago, paid for by the US Department of Labor and released in October 2020, found instead that 1.56 million children were working in cocoa in the two countries in 2018–19, 95 percent of them in hazardous work, and that child labour had risen since 2008–09 as production grew.

Girls are also moved within and into the country for work and sex. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says distant relatives bring girls from rural Côte d'Ivoire and other West African countries to Abidjan, promising school or training, and then keep them as domestic servants, where they are vulnerable to sexual exploitation. Ivorian women and girls are sold for sex, especially in Abidjan. Nigerian traffickers recruit women and girls with offers of jobs in shops and then exploit them in the gold-mining and cocoa regions, as part of networks that also move Nigerian girls to mines in Senegal, Mali and Burkina Faso.

Child labour in cocoa grew in the years when the industry had promised to reduce it. How many children in Côte d'Ivoire are sexually exploited is not known, because no representative survey has been done in West and Central Africa.

GBR.story:
Complaints about Jimmy Savile, a BBC presenter who also raised money for NHS hospitals, first reached the police in 1958. Police investigations during his lifetime, the last by Surrey Police in 2007–09, produced no charges, and in December 2011 after his death the BBC programme Newsnight shelved its own report on him. After an ITV documentary in October 2012, the Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree. Its 2013 report recorded 214 crimes from 1955 to 2009, and 73% of the 450 people who made allegations were under 18 at the time.

Cyril Smith, the Liberal MP for Rochdale from 1972 to 1992, was first reported to the police in 1968, by a pupil who was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man". The Director of Public Prosecutions, the official who decides on prosecutions, advised against charging him in 1970, and reviews in 1998 and 1999 brought no charge. He died in 2010, and in 2012 prosecutors said he should have been charged. In 2020 the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse (IICSA), a national inquiry for England and Wales with legal powers, found no organised network of abusers at Westminster but found "overt and direct deference by police towards powerful people".

In Rotherham, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited by groups of men between 1997 and 2013. It called the failures of the council and South Yorkshire Police "blatant", and three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Telford, a 2022 inquiry found more than 1,000 children exploited over at least 30 years, which agencies had treated as "child prostitution". In 2025 Baroness Casey's national audit found that police records were too poor to measure the scale of this abuse, and the government agreed to a new national inquiry with statutory powers.

IICSA's final report in 2022 made 107 recommendations. The first to be fully carried out, removing the three-year deadline for civil claims over child sexual abuse in England and Wales, took effect in June 2026, and the new inquiry into group-based exploitation is starting with Oldham.

GMB.story:
In 2003 The Gambia passed the Tourism Offences Act. It defined a child as anyone under 18, made hotel operators liable if they knowingly allowed child prostitution on their premises, and set life imprisonment as the penalty for tourists who traffic children. By 2017 the US State Department reported that traffickers were increasingly hosting foreign men who came to abuse children in private homes outside the main tourist areas, where they were harder to detect.

The State Department's 2025 trafficking report says European tourists, mainly from the United Kingdom, reportedly still travel to The Gambia to sexually exploit children. Organised networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country, and especially the Senegambia Strip, a beach resort area, to these visitors. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for jobs in tourism and then sexually exploited.

After the 2003 law, traffickers moved some of the abuse into private homes, and visitors from Europe still come for it. The number of children affected is not known, because no representative survey of child sexual exploitation has been done in West and Central Africa.

The extent of child sexual exploitation in Iran is therefore not known.

IRQ.story:
On 3 August 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State (ISIS) attacked Sinjar, the home district of the Yazidi religious minority in northern Iraq. Its fighters moved captured Yazidis by bus and truck to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul and Baaj, including Badoush prison and a wedding hall in Mosul, and then took women and girls to Raqqa in Syria. Women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at markets and held as sexual slaves, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. In June 2016 the UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found that ISIS had committed genocide against the Yazidis and that more than 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, most of them in Syria. Thousands remain missing.

After ISIS lost its territory, the risk to children moved into the camps for displaced people. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says women and girls in these camps whose relatives are accused of links to ISIS may be sexually exploited by security and military officials. An international organisation reported in 2024 that officials made family members of detained children perform sex acts in exchange for security clearances or civil documents, such as identity papers. The government reported no action against these officials. The same report says Yazidi survivors remain at risk of being trafficked again. Armed groups also still take children: the UN verified 18 abductions in 2022, 10 of them by ISIS and 4 by the Kurdish armed group HPG/PKK, and 8 in 2024.

Thousands of Yazidi women and children taken in 2014 are still missing. Children in the displacement camps whose families are linked to ISIS depend on officials for their papers, and some of those officials are accused of exploiting them. No representative survey has measured the sexual exploitation of children in the Middle East and North Africa.

ISL.story:
Iceland appears in the records for this map mainly as a place where abuse material is stored online. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds abuse images and has them removed, took action against 7,455 web addresses hosted on servers in Iceland, 2 percent of all the addresses it acted on that year.

The records also link Iceland to two international police operations in 2025. In Operation Stream, police from 38 countries working with Europol, the European Union's police agency, took down Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users, and identified 1,393 suspects. In Operation Cumberland, police from Denmark and 18 other countries acted against a paid platform that distributed abuse images made with artificial intelligence, identifying 273 suspects and arresting 25. Europol said many countries had no national laws covering such images.

Abuse material is still hosted on servers in Iceland. The records for this map hold no inquiry or count of abuse of children within the country.

ITA.story:
Italy has never held a national inquiry into the abuse of children in the Catholic Church or other institutions, and there are no official statistics on it. In May 2012 the Italian Bishops' Conference, the body of the country's Catholic bishops, said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty that governs relations between Italy and the Holy See, its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The victims' group Rete l'Abuso has asked for years for an independent inquiry.

Fr Nicola Corradi was accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, and the diocese flagged him in 2011. He continued working at the order's school in Luján de Cuyo in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016, and in 2019 a court in Mendoza convicted him of abusing deaf children there and sentenced him to 42 years. Joseph Henn, a priest indicted in Arizona in 2003, went to Italy and avoided extradition, the legal handing over of a suspect to another country, until he was arrested in Rome in May 2019.

Italy is also the destination of a trafficking route for women and girls, most of them from Edo State in Nigeria, who are moved overland through Niger and Libya and then by boat, bound by debts and oaths. The UN migration agency IOM recorded an almost 600 percent rise in potential victims arriving by sea between 2014 and 2017. In Palermo, police arrested 19 alleged members of a cell of Black Axe, a Nigerian confraternity, in 2016 over the exploitation of prostitution and other crimes; a judge convicted 14 in 2018, and in 2019 another court rejected the charge of mafia association against five others. In 2016 Europol, the European Union's police agency, said that at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy.

No national inquiry has counted abuse in Italy's churches and institutions, so its extent is not known. It is also not known how many of the 5,000 migrant children who went missing in Italy were exploited.

KEN.story:
In December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs published a study of four beach resort areas on the coast. It found that up to 30 percent of girls aged 12 to 18 living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex. Kenyans made up 38 percent of the clients, and tourists from Italy, Germany and Switzerland 44 percent. The vice president, Moody Awori, accepted the findings and said the police and communities had failed to enforce the law. A 2023 study by a charity, cited in the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report, estimated that more than 2,000 children were sold for sex in Kilifi and Kwale counties on the coast, now more often in private villas and holiday homes than in hotels. The same report described concerns about officials taking part, with no action reported against them.

Children are also sold in Nairobi. In 2020 a year-long investigation by BBC Africa Eye found people who snatched babies from homeless mothers and sold them for about £350 to £550, and illegal street clinics that sold newborns. A clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings, using the hospital's real transfer papers. The BBC said he appeared to keep his job. Rings also bring women and underage girls across the border from the Karamoja region of Uganda to Nairobi for domestic work or sex.

At the Nyumbani Children's Home in Nairobi, a Catholic charity's home for children with HIV that drew large donations from the United States, a 2021 investigation by the US aid agency USAID found claims that volunteers, caregivers and other children had raped children to be credible. A 2022 USAID memo said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006.

Twenty years after the government accepted the 2006 findings, children are still sold for sex on the coast, now mostly in private villas. No action has been reported against the officials accused of taking part.

KWT.story:
On 21 August 2025 Kuwait's telecommunications regulator temporarily blocked Roblox, an online game platform popular with children, after parents and community groups raised concerns about children's safety. Qatar had blocked it on 13 August and Turkey on 7 August, and Oman and Jordan had banned it since 2020.

Little else about the abuse or exploitation of children in Kuwait is counted. Childlight, a research centre that combines national surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that there was no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children for the Middle East and North Africa. Without such surveys, the only figures are cases that reach the police or are reported by technology companies.

The extent of child sexual exploitation in Kuwait is not known.

LUX.story:
Between 1984 and 2008, 561 children from South Korea were sent to Luxembourg for adoption, part of about 163,898 Korean children sent abroad from 1953 to 2008. Four Korean agencies held guardianship of the children and sent them abroad under government policy. In March 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body investigating past abuses, found that these agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet the demand of foreign partner agencies, had falsely registered children as orphans and had sometimes swapped children's identities, and that the Korean state had failed to supervise them.

Luxembourg is also linked in the records to Operation Stream, the 2025 police action by 38 countries and Europol, the European Union's police agency, against Kidflix, a paid streaming site for abuse videos with 1.8 million users. The operation identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79.

Some of the Korean children adopted in Luxembourg may have false records of their origins, according to the Korean commission's findings. The records for this map hold no inquiry by Luxembourg into these adoptions.

MAR.story:
In December 2010 Moroccan police arrested Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, and in September 2011 a court sentenced him to 30 years in prison for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. On 30 July 2013 King Mohammed VI pardoned him along with 47 other Spanish prisoners, as a gesture towards Spain. Galván left Morocco on an expired passport, with the authorities' knowledge. Protesters gathered outside parliament in Rabat and were violently dispersed. On 4 August the king revoked the pardon and said he had not been told the details of the case. Spanish police arrested Galván on 7 August, and he was imprisoned in Spain to finish his sentence. It was not the first such pardon. A 2010 US diplomatic cable reported that in 2006 the king had pardoned Hervé Le Gloannec, a Frenchman convicted of abusing a 15-year-old boy in Marrakesh, and he was released.

Foreign offenders still come to Morocco. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says foreign nationals, mainly from Europe and the Middle East, sexually exploit children in the major cities, and that charities report tourists abusing children in Tangier in holiday rentals owned and run by Europeans. It also reports alleged exploitation of children after the earthquake in Al Haouz in September 2023. Moroccan courts convicted 60 traffickers in 2024.

Morocco has also sent soldiers abroad as UN peacekeepers, and Moroccan military personnel are named in UN records of sexual exploitation and abuse allegations in the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Foreign men continue to abuse children in Moroccan cities, and in two known cases foreigners convicted of it were freed by royal pardon. How many children are affected is not known, because no representative survey of online or other exploitation has been done in the Middle East and North Africa.

MYS.story:
On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 children's homes in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan run as charities by Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), a company linked to Al-Arqam, a religious movement that is banned in Malaysia. Police had received 41 reports about the group since 2011 and had gathered intelligence for six months before the raids. They rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, and by 10 October the number of children rescued had risen to 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022 and 2023, another teaching assistant was charged with sexually assaulting four boys, and others were charged with physically abusing children. Police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

In 2016 an undercover investigation by Al Jazeera's 101 East programme found babies being advertised online with photographs and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by sex, race and skin colour. Some went to couples who wanted a child, and the programme reported that others were sold to traffickers. Among those giving up babies were immigrant sex workers, who are not legally allowed to bear children in Malaysia.

Malaysian servers also hold abuse material. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, took action against 17,046 web addresses hosted in Malaysia, 5 percent of its total, the same share as in 2024.

The GISB cases were at the charge stage in the records for this map, so the courts have not yet decided them. Malaysia's share of the world's hosted abuse material did not fall between 2024 and 2025.

NLD.story:
In March 2010 the Catholic Church in the Netherlands set up a commission led by the former minister Wim Deetman to examine abuse by its clergy. Its report in December 2011 identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who had abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated that 10,000 to 20,000 minors had been abused. It found that bishops and church officials had known and followed a policy of "not hanging out the dirty washing". In 2012 a state commission received 800 claims of sexual abuse in children's homes and foster families and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor.

The Netherlands also received thousands of children through intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. About 4,000 came from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, where babies were bought or taken from hospitals and handed to paid "acting mothers" who posed as birth mothers in court. A government committee chaired by Tjibbe Joustra reported in February 2021 that adoptions from Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia and other countries from 1967 to 1997/98 involved serious violations and that the Dutch government had failed for decades to prevent them. On 8 February 2021 the government suspended all intercountry adoption with immediate effect, and in 2024 announced that its citizens would no longer be allowed to adopt from abroad.

In 2018 the Netherlands held 47% of the material removed by the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images. Its share fell to 11% in 2025, or 33,788 web addresses, but INHOPE, the international network of reporting hotlines, still ranked it first for confirmed material that year.

The Netherlands has examined abuse in the church, in state care and in adoption, and has closed adoption from abroad. Its share of the abuse material found online has fallen, but Dutch servers still hold more confirmed material than those of any other country in INHOPE's count.

PRY.story:
In 2002 Fr Carlos Urrutigoity, an Argentine priest, was accused in the Diocese of Scranton in the United States of sleeping in the same beds as boarding-school students at St Gregory's Academy, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved with his group of followers to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este in Paraguay. In 2014 its bishop, Rogelio Livieres, made him vicar general, the bishop's second-in-command. Pope Francis removed Livieres later in 2014, reportedly in part because of this case, and in June 2015 Urrutigoity was moved again, to Mendoza in Argentina. He has not been convicted. The Paraguayan newspaper La Nación reported that at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or of crimes against humanity had taken shelter in Paraguay.

Paraguay has also been a place to live for offenders from abroad. In April 2021 police arrested a German man in Paraguay who was one of the administrators of Boystown, a website on the hidden part of the internet used to share the abuse of boys, which had 400,000 registered users. He and three other German administrators were sentenced in December 2022 to between 7 and 12 years.

Inside the country, the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report describes criadazgo, a common practice in which families take in children from poorer households and make them work as unpaid domestic servants. An estimated 47,000 children live in criadazgo, most of them girls, and many are highly vulnerable to sex and labour trafficking.

About 47,000 children remain in criadazgo, which the US government treats as a form of trafficking. Accused priests from neighbouring Argentina have found posts in Paraguay, and the records show none of them convicted there.

PSE.story:
In June 2024 the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, a body appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, reported on sexual violence in the war that began on 7 October 2023. It found that Israeli security forces had subjected Palestinians in detention and during arrests to sexual and gender-based violence, including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that "men and boys were targeted in particular ways". It found that the persecution of Palestinian men and boys on the basis of gender was a crime against humanity. The same commission found that sexual violence was committed in Israel on 7 October, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage.

In November 2025 the Palestinian authorities announced a ban on the online game platform Roblox, after several countries in the region blocked it over concerns about children's safety.

The UN commission's finding is the only official record on this map of sexual violence against Palestinian boys. Other abuse of children in Palestine is not measured, because no representative survey has been carried out in the Middle East and North Africa.

RWA.story:
Rwanda appears in the records for this map as a country that sent children abroad through intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. On 10 October 2007 Ireland's Adoption Board, the state body that then approved adoptions, suspended adoptions from Rwanda and Ethiopia.

The records give no further detail about adoptions from Rwanda, about the reasons for the suspension, or about the abuse or trafficking of children inside the country.
---

SSD.story:
In 2022 the UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls in South Sudan, some as young as seven. Soldiers of the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, the national army, were responsible for 74 of them, and armed opposition groups and the national police for most of the rest. In 2024 the UN verified seven cases, five of them by the army.

People displaced by the fighting shelter in UN-run camps called Protection of Civilians sites. In 2022 The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022, aid workers at the UN-run camp in Malakal had sexually exploited displaced women and girls, including by demanding sex in exchange for aid. Women and girls said they had been raped and become pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named. UN peacekeepers in South Sudan can be prosecuted only by the countries that sent them, and the UN can only send them home. In the UN's 2025 data on allegations against peacekeepers, few cases were finished: one Togolese officer was sent home and jailed for 60 days, and others were waiting for information from the country concerned.

Earlier, from 1994 to 2006, the Lord's Resistance Army, a Ugandan armed group, held children it had abducted in northern Uganda at its bases in southern Sudan. In 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, of 61 crimes including sexual slavery and forced marriage.

The UN records South Sudan's own army as the main abuser of girls there, and the records show no punishment of the aid workers named at Malakal. Online abuse is barely counted: in 2025 the US CyberTipline, which collects reports of online abuse from technology companies, received 863 reports for South Sudan.

SWE.story:
In February 2011 a Swedish government inquiry reported on abuse and neglect in municipal children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980. It recommended a public apology, which was made at Stockholm City Hall that year, and a payment of SEK 250,000 to each person who had suffered serious abuse. A compensation board opened in 2013, and by July 2015 it had decided just over 4,000 applications and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

Sweden was also one of the main receiving countries for intercountry adoption, the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. It took in 9,051 children from South Korea between 1957 and 2005. When South Korea tried to stop adoptions to Scandinavia in January 1975, the Swedish ambassador urged it to keep sending children. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, a state body investigating past abuses, found that Korean agencies had sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign demand and had registered children with known parents as orphans. Children also came to Sweden from Chile, where many were taken from poor mothers, some of whom were told their babies had died, from Sri Lanka in the 1980s, when babies were bought from "baby farms", and from Greece between 1950 and 1975.

After campaigning by Chilean adoptees, Sweden set up an independent inquiry. Its report of 2 June 2025, nearly 1,600 pages long, covered 65 years of adoptions and documented many irregular and illegal adoptions that state authorities had some knowledge of. By then Sweden had stopped adoptions from South Korea.

In 2016 Europol, the European Union's police agency, said that about 1,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared after arriving in Sweden, and that it had evidence some of the children who went missing in Europe had been sexually exploited.

Sweden has examined both its own care system and the adoptions it arranged from abroad, and found that state authorities knew of some of the illegal adoptions. The records for this map give no later account of the 1,000 migrant children who went missing in Sweden.

TUR.story:
Türkiye has hosted about 2.9 million people displaced from Syria. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says Syrian girls in Türkiye, especially in poor rural regions, are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, which are not registered with the state, and are then held as domestic servants and sold for sex. The report says corruption and official complicity remain significant concerns, but no investigations of complicit officials were reported.

Türkiye was earlier a destination for trafficking from Moldova. In March 2007 the State Department reported that women and children from Moldova were trafficked for sexual exploitation, more and more often to Russia and to the Middle East, including Türkiye, Israel and the United Arab Emirates. UNICEF found that children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more likely than other children to be trafficked.

In December 2025 prosecutors in Ankara reportedly opened an inquiry after an opposition MP, Turhan Çömez, cited US Justice Department files on Jeffrey Epstein. The document in question is a 2009 civil complaint by an anonymous woman that alleged, "upon information and belief", that Epstein had brought minor girls from Turkey and other countries. No findings or charges have been reported.

The forced marriage of Syrian girls in Türkiye continues, and no official has been investigated for taking part. The records for this map give no count of the girls affected.

UKR.story:
Between 2012 and 2015 the US-based group Disability Rights International investigated 33 Ukrainian orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities, and concluded that the orphanage system served traffickers as a way to recruit children. La Strada Ukraine, an anti-trafficking charity, told it that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution was "the most typical scheme", and that sexual exploitation in institutions usually began around age 13, often started by staff. A coordinator for IOM, the UN migration agency, said most documented trafficking cases began in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. In the same period Ukraine sent many children abroad for adoption: 18,612 between 2003 and 2022, and the United States issued visas to 10,544 children adopted from Ukraine from 1994 to 2014.

After Russia's full invasion in February 2022, Russian authorities moved children from occupied areas into Russia. In May 2022 President Vladimir Putin signed a decree that made it easier for Ukrainian children to receive Russian citizenship so that Russian families could adopt them, and Russia paid families for each child. Researchers at Yale University found at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea where at least 6,000 Ukrainian children were held for "re-education". In March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and for Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's children's rights commissioner, for the unlawful deportation and transfer of children. The UN verified the abduction of 122 children by Russian forces and authorities in 2022 and 2023, and a UN commission of inquiry found that Russian forces had raped children.

The war also put children left in Ukrainian institutions at risk. The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report said children evacuated from at least 195 facilities were at high risk, that officials at several state institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent, and that no complicit official had been convicted for the eighth year running.

By October 2026 Ukraine counted 20,651 children deported or forcibly displaced and 2,752 returned, so most have not come back. Children who remain in Ukraine's institutions are at risk from traffickers, and no official has been convicted of taking part.

VAT.story:
The Holy See is both the central government of the Catholic Church and a state with its own diplomats and courts. In 1922, and again in 1962 in an instruction called Crimen sollicitationis, it ordered that church trials of priests accused of sexual acts with children be kept absolutely secret, on pain of automatic excommunication. In 2001 it required bishops to send every case of a cleric's sexual offence with a minor to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, its office for church discipline, and kept those cases under the pontifical secret, its highest level of confidentiality. Between 2004 and 2013 that office studied 3,420 credible cases and dismissed 884 priests from the priesthood.

In August 2013 it recalled Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, its nuncio, or ambassador, to the Dominican Republic, amid allegations that he had abused minors, before Dominican prosecutors opened their investigation. He was charged by a Vatican prosecutor in 2015 and died before trial. In 2017 it recalled Mgr Carlo Capella from its embassy in Washington, and in 2018 its own court convicted him of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years; he was not tried in the United States or Canada. Archbishop Luigi Ventura, its nuncio to France, was tried in Paris in his absence and in December 2020 received an eight-month suspended sentence. Ireland's Murphy Commission, a state inquiry, received no files from the Vatican.

In 2014 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child said the Holy See had placed the church's reputation and the protection of offenders above children's interests and had moved abusive priests to new parishes. In 2019 Pope Francis required clergy to report suspected abuse to church authorities, though not to the police, and in December 2019 he lifted the pontifical secret so that case files could be given to state authorities.

Since December 2019 church files on abuse can be given to state authorities, but the Holy See still decides whether to hand them over, and its own rules do not require clergy to report abuse to the police.

WSM.story:
Between 2002 and 2005 Focus on Children, an adoption agency in Utah run by Scott and Karen Banks, arranged for about 80 Samoan children to be taken to the United States. The agency told the parents that their children would go to America for a time to attend school. Instead, the children were adopted permanently by American families. In February 2007 a US federal court charged the Banks and three others with alien smuggling, visa fraud and money laundering. In January 2009 they all pleaded guilty to misdemeanour charges, the less serious class of crime, of helping foreigners enter the country improperly, and the agency pleaded guilty to a more serious conspiracy charge. A judge sentenced them to five years' probation and banned them from adoption work. None went to prison.

A Salesian priest, a member of a Catholic religious order, who had been convicted of abuse in Melbourne, Australia, was allegedly moved to Samoa so that he would not face further police investigation.

Families in Samoa lost children to adoption abroad through an agency that misled them, and the people responsible were given probation. The case of the priest sent from Australia is an allegation, and the records do not show whether it was investigated in Samoa.

ZAF.story:
In 1979 Fettes College, a private school in Edinburgh, dismissed the teacher Iain Wares but gave him a glowing reference. He went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children. South Africa approved his extradition, the legal handing over of a suspect to another country, to Scotland, and in 2025 he was still contesting it. A German priest, Fr Georg Kerkhoff, also worked in South Africa for years while abuse cases were pending against him at home. He was tried in South Africa for abusing boys at a camp in 2008, then extradited to Germany and jailed in Krefeld in 2015.

The British barrister John Smyth came to South Africa from Zimbabwe. An internal report by the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity whose holiday camps he chaired, described in 1982 how he had beaten boys, and he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 without the police being told. When Zimbabwe refused to let him back into the country, he moved to South Africa in 2001. He was never charged anywhere. A review for the Church of England published in 2024 called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa" and found it highly likely that he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town in 2018.

Inside South Africa, the US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas and sell them for sex in the cities, especially in Gauteng and the Western Cape. Brothel owners use drugs to control them, some parents sell their own children for money or drugs, and low-level officials are complicit. In a separate case against Timothy Omotoso, which began in 2017, the trial was delayed for eight years by motions and recusals, and the witness Pamela Mabini, who had reported him, was shot dead on 7 March 2025, weeks before the verdict.

Abusers who left Britain and Germany found new work with children in South Africa, and two were later extradited or approved for extradition. The trafficking of rural children into the cities continues, with officials still complicit.

ZWE.story:
Between 1946 and 1956, 276 children from British care were sent to the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College in Southern Rhodesia, as Zimbabwe was then called, under British child migration programmes. These were schemes, backed by the UK government and run by charities such as the Fairbridge Society, that sent children from Britain to the colonies and dominions. At the college, children who told the headmaster that a padre, a chaplain, had sexually abused them were beaten and warned against "spreading malicious lies". In 2018 the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse for England and Wales called child migration "a deeply flawed government policy".

In 1984 the English barrister John Smyth moved to Zimbabwe. Two years earlier, an internal report for the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity whose holiday camps he had chaired, had described how he beat boys, but its readers did not tell the police. In Zimbabwe he founded Zambesi Ministries in 1986, which ran camps for boys. A 16-year-old died at one of the camps in December 1992. Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged. A review for the Church of England published in 2024 found no evidence that anyone in England had tried to warn the Zimbabwean authorities about him, and described him as "a problem solved and exported to Africa". Zimbabwe later refused to let him back into the country, and in 2001 he moved to South Africa.

The US State Department's 2025 trafficking report says women and children are sold for sex around Zimbabwe's gold and diamond mines, sometimes for money or food, and that children work there as panners and ore carriers. Some families trade daughters for food or money, and under the custom of ngozi a girl may be given to another family to make amends for a killing. Low-level officials are complicit.

In both cases, British institutions that knew of abuse did not act to protect children in Zimbabwe. The risks the records describe today come from inside the country, where girls are traded by families and sold for sex around the mines.
